name: Testosterone gel (AndroGel)

lead: Testosterone gel is a prescription gel applied to the skin to treat low testosterone in men; AndroGel is the best-known brand. Its appearance interest comes from muscle and body composition: leaner, more muscular physiques once levels are restored.

The chain: testosterone is absorbed through the skin, circulating levels rise, and lean mass tends to go up while fat mass goes down. Studies in hypogonadal men report normalised testosterone and improvements in sexual function, mood, lean mass and bone density. Cosmetic use in men with normal levels is off-label and less studied.

paras: It is used as a daily gel under a prescriber's direction, often by men who want a steady alternative to injections. Lab monitoring is part of routine care, and body-composition changes in trials build over months.

Reported effects include acne, breast enlargement, raised hematocrit and sperm suppression, with cardiovascular and clot concerns discussed for testosterone products. Skin contact can transfer it to women and children, and virilisation has occurred in exposed people. It is a controlled substance needing a prescription in most countries.

angle.text: Testosterone gel is prescribed for diagnosed low testosterone, and users discuss it as a TRT option for muscle, body composition and energy. Trials in hypogonadal men show gains in lean mass and drops in fat mass; use for looks in men with normal levels is off-label.

lead: Testosterone gel is a prescription topical form of testosterone replacement therapy, rubbed onto the skin so that the hormone is absorbed into the bloodstream. It is sold under brand names including AndroGel, Testim, TestoGel and Fortesta, and has become the most popular testosterone form for hypogonadism in the United States [1]. It is prescribed mainly for male hypogonadism, in which the body makes too little testosterone, and it is also used in masculinising hormone therapy for transgender men [1][2].

The appearance interest comes from what normal testosterone levels do to body composition. In a 2004 study of 163 hypogonadal men followed for up to 42 months, continuous gel use normalised average testosterone, increased lean mass, reduced fat mass and improved bone density, although muscle strength did not rise significantly [3]. Those changes were measured in men with diagnosed low testosterone. In muscle- and appearance-focused communities the gel is discussed as a steadier, needle-free alternative to injections within testosterone replacement therapy (TRT), rather than as a cosmetic product [4][5].

The research base is large for a prescription hormone. It includes the 5,246-man TRAVERSE cardiovascular safety trial of a 1.62 percent gel [6], the 790-man Testosterone Trials in older men [7], a prostate-safety analysis [8], and a long-term sexual-function study [9]. Regulators describe the benefits and risks of testosterone for age-related decline differently from its use in diagnosed hypogonadism: the US FDA stated in 2015 that benefit and safety for age-related low testosterone had not been established [1]. Testosterone is a controlled substance in many countries [1].

paras: The primary indication is testosterone replacement in men with hypogonadism, meaning symptoms together with consistently low testosterone levels. Masculinising therapy for transgender men is a further use, and a registered study covers sex-steroid replacement in hypogonadal and transgender active-duty patients [1][2]. Testosterone is also used for certain breast cancers, and it is on the WHO Essential Medicines List [1].

Gels avoid injections, and transdermal gel became the most popular form for hypogonadism in the US [1]. A 2020 American College of Physicians guideline cited on Wikipedia suggested intramuscular rather than transdermal treatment on the basis of similar effectiveness and harms with lower cost, so injectable and gel forms are both in routine use [1].

Interest in appearance centres on muscle, fat distribution, skin and energy. The 2004 AndroGel study reported benefits for sexual function, mood, lean and fat mass and bone mineral density in hypogonadal men [3]. The chain people describe is more testosterone, more lean tissue and less fat, and a leaner, more muscular physique; the study found lean mass up and fat mass down but no significant strength gain [3].

Those findings were in men with diagnosed low testosterone and do not address use in men with normal levels. The Testosterone Trials in men aged 65 and over with low levels and symptoms found improved sexual activity, desire and erectile function with one year of gel, a smaller benefit for mood, and no benefit for vitality or walking distance, though the trial was too small to settle questions of risk [7].

The long-term hypogonadism data are the most direct: the 2004 study normalised testosterone, and a 2024 analysis nested in TRAVERSE enrolled 1,161 men with low libido and found that gel improved sexual activity, hypogonadal symptoms and desire over two years but did not improve erectile function [3][9]. An earlier trial reported that adding gel helped erectile dysfunction in men with acquired androgen deficiency who had not responded to sildenafil alone [10]. A 2002 study examined testosterone replacement for non-motor symptoms of Parkinson disease [11], and a randomised trial tested a 1 percent gel in women with poor response to IVF [12]. A review of the role of testosterone in menopausal hormone treatment discusses its use for low sexual desire in postmenopausal women; no testosterone product is approved for women in the US [13][1].

Applied gel delivers testosterone through the skin into the circulation. A randomised crossover study in 29 hypogonadal men compared a single application of Testim with AndroGel and found higher peak and total exposure with Testim, so the authors concluded the two 1 percent gels were not bioequivalent [14]. A later record review of 370 men found that 20 percent changed gel brand after a poor initial response; men who moved from AndroGel to Testim had higher average testosterone afterwards, and the authors suggested that switching brand might be worth trying before abandoning therapy [15].

Testosterone is highly protein-bound, with 97 to 99.5 percent attached to sex hormone-binding globulin and albumin, and is mainly metabolised in the liver; a small share is converted to estradiol, and the gel also slightly raises dihydrotestosterone [1][3]. Oral testosterone has very low bioavailability because of extensive first-pass liver metabolism [1]. Other brand and non-gel forms include Androderm patches, Axiron solution, Natesto nasal gel and injectables such as Xyosted and Aveed [1].

Testosterone products can cause acne, oily skin, fluid retention and breast enlargement in men. Serious effects reported across the class include liver toxicity, blood clots, raised hematocrit and worsening of sleep apnea or benign prostatic hyperplasia [1]. In the 2004 study, hematocrit and hemoglobin rose as expected, local skin irritation occurred in 12 men and only one stopped treatment because of it; three men with raised PSA had prostate cancer on biopsy, though the study was not designed to assess cancer risk and the authors advised monitoring [3].

Because exogenous testosterone suppresses gonadotropins and the testes' own testosterone, it reduces sperm production; recovery after stopping is variable, and exogenous testosterone is contraindicated in men trying to conceive [16][1]. Medical therapies including hCG and selective estrogen receptor modulators are used in some patients to preserve fertility [16]. Researchers have also studied testosterone-based regimens in male hormonal contraception [17].

Skin contact can pass testosterone to others. Women and children exposed to the hormone can develop virilisation, and testosterone is contraindicated in pregnancy [1]. A 2022 news story about a two-year-old showing signs of puberty after exposure to his father's gel circulated widely on Hacker News [18].

The cardiovascular question was tested in TRAVERSE, a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled noninferiority trial of 5,246 men aged 45 to 80 with existing or high risk of cardiovascular disease and low testosterone, who used a 1.62 percent gel or placebo. Major adverse cardiac events occurred in 7.0 percent on testosterone and 7.3 percent on placebo (hazard ratio 0.96), meeting the noninferiority margin, while atrial fibrillation, acute kidney injury and pulmonary embolism were more frequent on testosterone [6]. A prostate-safety analysis of the same trial found high-grade prostate cancer in 0.19 percent on testosterone and 0.12 percent on placebo, a difference that was not statistically significant, though PSA rose more on testosterone [8].

In February 2025 the FDA changed testosterone labelling, removing language about adverse cardiovascular outcomes from the boxed warning, citing TRAVERSE, and adding a warning about increased blood pressure [1]. Registered studies have used ambulatory blood pressure monitoring in men on gel and other testosterone products [19][20][21]. Earlier, in 2014, the FDA opened a review of cardiovascular risk and added warnings about deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism [1].

The 2004 open-label study followed 163 hypogonadal men on 1 percent gel for up to 42 months, 123 of whom were evaluable; it reported normalised testosterone and sustained improvements in sexual function, mood, lean mass, fat mass and bone density, with gains in spine density exceeding those in the hip [3]. A three-year preliminary report also followed hypogonadal men on gel [22]. A 2010 comparison examined clomiphene citrate versus gel for hypogonadism, including cost [23], and a 2016 study found that oral enclomiphene raised testosterone and preserved sperm counts in obese hypogonadal men, unlike topical testosterone [24].

The Testosterone Trials randomised 790 men aged 65 or older with low testosterone to gel or placebo for a year and measured sexual function, physical function and vitality [7]. TRAVERSE enrolled 5,246 men, with mean treatment of 21.7 months and mean follow-up of 33 months [6]. Registered trials include a Phase 4 study of AndroGel in men with type 2 diabetes and hypogonadism, a Phase 1 study of testosterone replacement in low-risk prostate cancer, and blood pressure monitoring studies of Vogelxo and Androderm [25][26][20][21].

Testosterone was isolated in 1935 and approved for medical use in 1939 [1]. US use of testosterone roughly tripled between 2001 and 2011, with transdermal gels becoming the most popular formulation for hypogonadism [1]. Testim pharmacokinetics were compared with AndroGel in a 2003 study, and by 2004 AndroGel had accumulated multi-year safety and efficacy data [14][3]. In 2023, testosterone ranked among the most commonly prescribed drugs in the United States, with more than 5 million prescriptions [1].

Testosterone is Schedule III in the United States since the 1990 Anabolic Steroid Control Act, Schedule IV in Canada, Class C in the UK and prescription-only in the EU, and the World Anti-Doping Agency bans it in sport [1]. Claims analyses have studied adherence to topical testosterone in hypogonadal men [27]. By 2014 lawsuits had alleged increased rates of stroke and heart attack in older men using testosterone supplements [1].

On looksmax.org a member posts about having ordered TestoGel, and T Nation hosts discussion of TRT protocols, hCG and testicular atrophy [4][5][28]. Members of these communities discuss obtaining TRT through clinics and online channels, and the wiki gives no sourcing or dosing details.

lore.intro: Testosterone gel is discussed in muscle and looksmaxxing forums mainly as a form of TRT, with threads about getting started, protocol questions and fertility side effects [4][5][28].

claims.claim: Gel is a gentler, steadier way to do TRT than injections.
TRT builds lean muscle and cuts fat.
TRT is only for men with proven low testosterone.
TRT can be paired with hCG or other drugs to protect fertility and testes.
Skin contact can transfer gel to partners and children.
